A pram is a small, four-wheeled vehicle designed to carry a baby. A parent or caregiver pushes it from behind using a handle while walking. The baby lies flat inside it, comfortably and safely, often covered by a hood or canopy to protect from sun, wind, or rain.

Think of it as a cozy, wheeled bed for a baby that can be taken outdoors.

A pram typically has:

  • A deep, basket-like body — large enough for a baby to lie fully flat, like a mini bed on wheels.
  • Four wheels — usually large and sturdy, good for rolling on pavements and paths.
  • A long handle — so the person pushing it can walk upright comfortably behind it.
  • A hood or canopy — which folds up or down to shield the baby from the elements.

The baby inside a pram almost always faces the person who is pushing it, so the parent and baby can see each other. This is an important detail, as you'll see below.
How Is a Pram Different from a Stroller or Buggy?

This is where many learners get confused, so pay close attention.

A pram, a stroller, and a buggy all carry babies, but they are not exactly the same thing.

Pram vs. Stroller:
A pram is for very young babies — newborns and infants who cannot yet sit up on their own. Because these babies must lie flat, a pram has a deep, bed-like seat. A stroller (called a pushchair in British English), on the other hand, is for older babies and toddlers who can sit up. Its seat is upright, not flat. The baby in a stroller typically faces away from the pusher, looking forward at the world.

So, in short: pram = baby lies flat, faces the pusher. Stroller = baby sits up, faces forward.

Pram vs. Buggy:
A buggy is generally a lighter, more compact, and foldable version of a pushchair/stroller. It's designed for convenience and travel. A pram, by contrast, is heavier and bulkier but offers more comfort for a very young baby.

"Pram" is primarily British English. You will hear and read this word most commonly in the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, and other countries that use British English.

In American English, people rarely say "pram." Instead, Americans say "baby carriage" or "baby buggy" for the same object. If you are reading a British novel, watching a British film, or speaking with someone from the UK, you will almost certainly encounter the word "pram."

The word "pram" has a second, much less common meaning — a type of small, flat-bottomed boat. It has a squared-off front end (called a blunt bow) rather than a pointed one. This kind of pram is used as a small rowing boat or as a dinghy (a small boat used to get to and from a larger boat). You might encounter this meaning in sailing or nautical contexts, but in everyday conversation, "pram" almost always refers to the baby carriage.
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

Here are some natural examples to help you "feel" the word in real use:

  • "She parked the pram outside the café while she went in to order coffee."
  • "The newborn slept peacefully in his pram as his mother walked through the park."
  • "Don't leave the baby in the pram unattended."
  • "We need to buy a pram before the baby arrives."

There is also a famous British idiom: "to throw one's toys out of the pram" — meaning to react to a situation in an immature, childish way, like a baby throwing a tantrum. For example: "He threw his toys out of the pram when he didn't get the promotion."

What it isA four-wheeled baby carriage where the baby lies flat
Who uses itParents/caregivers of newborns and young infants
Where the word is usedMainly British English (UK, Australia, NZ, etc.)
American English equivalentBaby carriage / baby buggy
Key difference from strollerPram = flat/lying position; Stroller = upright/sitting position
Secondary meaningA small, flat-bottomed boat (nautical context)

That's everything you need to know about the word pram. It's a simple, practical word, but knowing its regional roots, its distinctions from similar words, and its idiomatic use puts you well ahead of most learners.
